  • Sources indicate that this Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: The BBC's Katya Adler speaks to protesters taking part in recent demonstrations.

France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.

Sources indicate that this Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.

President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he notes, is to bring down the French Republic.

That's quite a claim â and one that needs examining.

Recent findings suggest that the unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.

So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?

Industry observers note that it's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.

Sources indicate that my best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.

Sources indicate that you see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.

The BBC's Katya Adler talking to a protester.

Sources indicate that french intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article, external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around â¬207m (Â£175.5m).

Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.

It has been revealed that towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.

French police pepper spraying protesters during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris earlier this month.

As we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they stated.

Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police â they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype.

"How can you justify the violence?" I ask them.

"Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard.".

Recent findings suggest that "We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight.".

These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.

Recent findings suggest that they weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.

Left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block, tend to dress in all black, wearing ski masks or balaclavas.

Earlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.

I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.

They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again â would only speak if they could remain anonymous.

Industry observers note that "Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society.".

How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?

In a recent development, they shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.

Some protesters don't support the Black Block's violence but say the state's violence is worse.

French intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.

Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.

Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.

Sources indicate that he highlighted me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt.

"We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me.

"We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw.".

I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?

In a recent development, as he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do.

Industry observers note that "The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution.

Industry observers note that "Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us.".

When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change.

Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests.

"The Black Block isn't a single organisation," claims protester Starflix.

There are numerous websites and Instagram profiles, mainly hosted by left-wing organisations, offering tips for protesters and rioters, such as: keep your phone at home so police can't track you, cover your face to avoid being identified and emulate martial arts expert Bruce Lee and "be like water" - appearing and disappearing into crowds. That's advice passed on by the Hong Kong protesters eight years ago.

While not formally organising the protests or violence with these posts, could the fact groups host this information online be viewed as a kind of incitement or manipulation of youngsters whose feelings are running so high in France?

All the young rioters I spoke to insist they are not being herded or directed, but is there something bigger behind what's happening?

Ultra-left protesters spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity.

It takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true?

"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within.".

Sources indicate that "Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage and not just in France. You see the same rage [in protests] in Italy, Germany, Spain. It's exploding by itself.".

Industry observers note that I ask if the anti-capitalist presidential candidate Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon and his France Unbowed party (LFI) are somehow linked to the violence. They are present at most protests, supporters handing out campaign pamphlets to the chanting crowds.

But the activist denies this, telling me MÃ©lenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He notes the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch".

Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to collapse the French government?

"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people.

"More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol.".

You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left.

Limoges Town Hall, allegedly damaged by protesters, has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in.

In a recent development, this is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month. The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on.

Recent findings suggest that the 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak.

Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous.

"We were all shocked by the [town hall] fire â even as we watched it happen in front of us - but it's our duty to take action," he tells me.

Sources indicate that "I can't leave this world to my son in the state that it's in. Look how military vehicles and brute force are used by the state against our young students.

It has been revealed that "It's amazing the people haven't taken up arms against them. Do we need a policeman killed in order for the state to listen?".

How can you say that, I want to know?

"As a child, I was educated with French values â liberty, equality, fraternity - but when I look at the social injustice in the world now, I'm disgusted. As a father, I can't let this go on. If I have to, I would take a bullet to protect the youth of this country.".

These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France.

Upcoming presidential elections offer a crossroad, with polls predicting a run-off between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon.

In a recent development, we repeatedly approached French intelligence. They didn't want to comment. A sign perhaps of the huge sensitivity of the current situation, especially with France hurtling towards an extremely charged presidential election.

But Michel Klein, a recently retired former police commissioner, told me he didn't think the radical left posed a serious threat to the French state.

"I believe there is a will from the radical left and the anarchists to try and destroy the Republic but they obviously don't have the means to do it," he told me.

He sees no risk of civil war in France (a possibility you hear some in the country discuss these days) but he identified a rising risk of clashes between far-left and far-right groups ahead of the presidential election.

Polls at the moment predict a run-off in the vote between nationalist candidate Marine Le Pen and anticapitalist MÃ©lenchon.

Far-right vigilante groups have begun appearing on the edge of protests in a number of cities across France to "protect French streets", they say.

The popular hard-left presidential candidate MÃ©lenchon attends most demos, his supporters handing political pamphlets to the chanting crowds, but he denies any links with violence.

Sources indicate that france is so polarised, there's little sign next year's presidential vote will calm things. This turbulent mix of left and right, social and political unrest, feels like a perfect storm.

Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?

The biggest downsides to using Apple's Magic Mouse

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple switched the Magic Mouse to USB-C but left its most questionable design decision untouched, and that isn’t the only thing owners dislike.
  • There are a handful of things that Apple's Magic Mouse does that would make regular mice envious.
  • Sources indicate that and it isn't the only reason even committed Mac users are calling it quits on the official Apple mouse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple switched the Magic Mouse to USB-C but left its most questionable design decision untouched, and that isn’t the only thing owners dislike.

There are a handful of things that Apple's Magic Mouse does that would make regular mice envious. The shimmery Multi-Touch surface lets you scroll sideways on a spreadsheet and move across macOS even without that conventional scroll wheel. But then, it is also brilliantly designed to be unusable when the charging cable is plugged in. That's not a small trade-off, especially for a device whose very purpose is to make computer use a breeze.

Sources indicate that and it isn't the only reason even committed Mac users are calling it quits on the official Apple mouse. The weirdly slender body looks gorgeous but offers barely any palm space, while the aluminum sides aren't universally loved either. For those who've used a traditional mouse for years, the controls on the Magic Mouse can also feel severely limiting.

According to recent reports, even after ditching the Lightning port with the 2024 refresh alongside the much faster M4 iMac, Apple decided to leave most of those pain points untouched. Now, in all honesty, the Magic Mouse has a pretty strong fan base, especially among consumers who love its touch gestures and that classic Apple minimalist design. But if you're spending hours using it, the things it cuts out can matter a lot more than the cool tricks it has.

According to recent reports, apple unveiled the rechargeable Magic Mouse 2 back in October 2015 with its Lightning port at the bottom. A seemingly controversial design choice even back then, it somehow survived the switch to USB-C almost a decade later. So, every time your Magic Mouse is out of juice, you need to flip it over and leave it be until there's enough power to start using the mouse again.

Industry observers note that the saving grace here is that the mouse's battery is good for around a month or more between charges, so flipping your Magic Mouse on its back isn't a daily ordeal. But that doesn't make it any less weird, especially since Apple allows its Magic Keyboard and Magic Trackpad to be used while they're plugged in. There's also no clarity from Apple on how many years the rechargeable battery in the Magic Mouse is expected to last.

Now, let's talk about that shape which puts this slim mouse at just 0.85 inches tall. There's also barely any palm support, and depending on how you're holding it, those aluminum edges can press uncomfortably against your fingers. If you use a fingertip grip, this might be less of a problem, but if you're more of a "resting your entire hand on a mouse" type of person, adjusting your grip is something you'll have to get used to.

Recent findings suggest that since Apple is asking $79 for the Magic Mouse in white and $99 for the black version, you'd expect the basic functions. While Apple's mouse supports right-clicking with its touch-sensitive surface, there's no middle-click or a programmable thumb button. Using CAD software is where you miss those buttons the most, since holding the middle mouse button is how you usually pan around drawings. Sure, third-party utilities can add some of the missing functionality, but having to install extra software to bring conventional features to a premium mouse is frustrating to say the least.

Recent findings suggest that you've got to give some credit to the Multi-Touch surface, especially for making scrolling without the usual wheel still feel natural. But do expect accidental swipes like you would on a phone screen since there are no physical controls. Some owners have even faced challenges like stuttering and inconsistent tracking. Those could very well be isolated incidents though, and in one case, the lag started right after a macOS update.

Recent findings suggest that the good part is that Apple doesn't force the Magic Mouse down your throat just because you own a Mac. You can use one of the best wireless mice from other brands on macOS, although you would be missing out on gestures that make the Magic Mouse so special. Logitech's Signature M650, for instance, packs a typical scroll wheel and comes equipped with physical side buttons. Costing about half as much as the Magic Mouse at $39.99, the M650 comes with a contoured grip in place of the Magic Mouse's glossy finish.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At least 23 people were injured in Colombia on Monday night when a car bomb tore through the central city of Villavicencio, local authorities confirmed on Tuesday.

The explosion occurred at approximately 9:30 p.m. (3:30 a.m. CET Tuesday) in front of the headquarters of the regional government of Meta province and caused severe structural damage to nearby buildings.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella confirmed the incident and mentioned no deaths had been reported "so far.".

Reporters for the AFP news agency said the blast knocked out power across parts of the city center, leaving damaged cars lining nearby streets and ripping open shopfronts.

Industry observers note that "The doors were bent in, the windows shattered, some display cases inside broken," remarked local resident Johan Perez, who owns a hat shop. "We are alive by a miracle.".

The Spanish EFE news agency reported that a well-known local restaurant was completely destroyed and suggested that the structural integrity of the government building itself may have been compromised, raising concerns that it could collapse.

The attack has not been publicly claimed by any group but it came on the eve of the 10th anniversary of Colombia's landmark peace accord with FARC guerrillas.

The agreement persuaded the FARC, once Latin America's largest guerrilla army, to lay down its weapons after more than half a century of conflict.

Shortly before Monday's blast, President De la Espriella had denounced the peace accord as a "false peace.".

According to the local Caracol radio station, investigators' initial theories point to a FARC commander known as "Antonio Medina" who leads the dissidents' 28th and 39th fronts, known as the "Amazonas Bloc.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

President De La Espriella, who took office in August and has launched a United States-backed military offensive against armed groups and drug traffickers, blamed "narco-terrorists" for the attack.

"I warn the narco-terrorists responsible: you will answer for every drop of blood you have spilled and every business and property you have destroyed," he wrote on social media.

"We will deploy the full power of the state to hunt you down, dismantle your organizations and take you out." De La Espriella added.

The incident marks the latest violent resurgence of a conflict that has shaken Colombia, the world's largest cocaine-producing nation, over the past two years.

Between January and November, authorities recorded 358 drone strikes, more than one a day, according to a Defense Ministry document obtained by AFP.

Last year, a presidential candidate was assassinated on the campaign trail.

#173275. Tech Report: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1175 w)

Tech Report: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade.
  • Industry observers note that xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024.
  • As of October 2026, data center developers have revealed prepares for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

Industry observers note that xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have revealed prepares for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a upcoming industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

It has been revealed that rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some crucial questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” states Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont notes.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

In a recent development, the on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.).

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi claims. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of unveiled projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

According to recent reports, and while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, claims Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Recent findings suggest that creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi indicates. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”.

What strike on Russian ship in Libya indicates about spread of Ukraine war

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack.
  • The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU security agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
  • Industry observers note that the answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU security agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?

Industry observers note that the answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.

Russia, which is at the moment engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".

It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.

Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks â what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" â have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.

In a recent development, it's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

How Ukraine drone attacks on Russian ships unfolded.

Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.

If Ukraine can initiative and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?

As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.

On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.

This, remarked Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.

It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.

But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much â but not all â of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.

Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland claims airspace violated by Russian missile.

Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.

In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.

The three Baltic states â Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania â all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.

There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.

Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.

Hybrid warfare isn't fresh but it is on the rise.

It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.

Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted in August by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.

There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Best espresso machines for home must thread a delicate needle. Espresso is forceful and finicky, and a little intimidating, and yet so essential that astronauts might take it into orbit. A home espresso machine remains the most intense and expensive device I regularly operate before my first cup of coffee.

It has been revealed that I tend to favor devices that let technology do much of the work and don’t make you join a cult of engineers before your first cup. And so my top-rated espresso machine, the Fellow Series 1, earned its place on WIRED’s counter by combining ease of use with a solid build, consistent temperature, and rare control over pressure—an industry-beating mix of nerdiness and hand-holding friendliness. For a more classic, all-analog build, we offer the compact, stylish Diletta Mio.

It has been revealed that but I know not everyone wants to also buy a good coffee grinder or spend four figures for their morning cup. For those who want milk-based drinks and a built-in grinder, I recommend the top-selling Breville Barista Express as the Goldilocks machine balancing performance and cost. For an entry-level device, I pretty much always recommend the straight-ahead Breville Bambino, among the lowest-cost machines with PID-controlled temperature.

According to recent reports, note that this guide mostly covers classic, hands-on espresso machines with portafilters. We do also include the De'Longhi Rivelia, our top pick among super-automatic espresso machines that require little more than a button press. For a guide that focuses on easy-to-use espresso machine picks that do most of the work for you, check out our guide to the Best Latte and Automatic Espresso Machines.

Also, be sure to check out our other coffee guides, like the Best Drip Coffee Makers, Best Cold Brew Makers, Best Aeropresses, Best Coffee Pod Machines, Best Coffee Subscriptions, and Best Coffee Grinders.

Updated November 2026: We’ve added information on Meraki’s second-run release and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

It has been revealed that san Francisco-based Fellow is almost certainly the most innovative and tech-forward coffee machine organization of the moment. And rarely has an espresso machine so swiftly changed what I want from the best espresso makers as the Fellow Series 1, which started shipping in early 2026. Sure, the temperature control is admirable, with a patented heating technology that threads the needle between the fast heating of a thermoblock and the stability of a boiler. Automatic milk frothing is about as good and as fast as it gets. The dial and LED-screen controls are intuitive. And the device is compact, conserving both counter space and airspace.

But the real game-changing addition with this machine is the way Fellow has introduced tight pressure control and shot profiles to the non-geek home espresso landscape. Almost every other espresso machine on the market just sorta aims at 9 bars of pressure and shrugs. The Series 1 offers profiles for light, medium, or dark roast that change pressure based on what's right for each bean—keeping dark roasts classic but pulling longer shots and dialing back pressure on light-roast beans. Other profiles, like turbo shots or “Modern Arc,” cater to the modern yen for espresso with less bitterness.

After testing for weeks, I'm sold. You'd pay at least double to find this feature on any other espresso machine. And no device lets you play with pressure as easily as the Fellow, even before a planned firmware update that'll allow you to sync profiles through Fellow's phone app. The app remains mostly a placeholder for now, offering tutorials and education but TBD functionality. But Fellow's track record building out the app on my top-pick drip coffee machine, the Fellow Aiden, gives me confidence this is a temporary blip. Volumetric controls still need tweaking, and the removable water reservoir can only be removed straight up from the device, requiring significant clearance.

But even with these early quirks, the Fellow Series 1 remains the most impressive espresso machine I've tested in the past couple of years. And it's changed what I want from espresso machines in the future. The Series 1 might already be the most-hyped machine of 2026. But this time, the hype is warranted.

The Barista Express had been our top pick for years, a Goldilocks choice in terms of price, versatility, and performance. It remains among the most popular espresso machines in the world (and possibly the most popular, period) for good reason. The Barista Express produces consistent pressure for espresso, its steam wand is excellent, and the built-in grinder makes it an all-in-one device. Its mostly metal construction, easy cleaning, and other thoughtful touches make it a faithful companion. My WIRED colleague Julian Chokkattu has been using his machine happily for seven years. And its price, which drops regularly during sales events, makes it accessible to mere mortals. For those who want a built-in grinder but don't want to spend four figures, this is an easy recommendation.

It has been revealed that competitors have taken direct aim at the Express with impressive semiautomatic entries like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier ($599) and Luxe Cafe Pro (see below), plus the De'Longhi La Specialista Opera ($900). Each of these offers more options, including cold espresso, with similar grind quality. For now, WIRED's years of testing and vetting the Barista Express, and Breville's good customer service reputation, keep the Express as my top recommendation. But in the meantime, I wouldn't be sad to see the Barista Express updated to better Baratza burrs on that built-in grinder, as Breville has done with its more expensive machines.

Upgrade pick: The Barista Express is a great mix of price and performance. But Breville's true top-line semiautomatic machine is the Breville Oracle Jet ($1,980 on Amazon), a touchscreen device with a better grinder that'll also offer better control and easier milk frothing and can guide you through everything from the proper bean grind to how to make a proper flat white, cappuccino, or espresso martini.

Industry observers note that A classic espresso machine rewards effort with nuance and beauty. And the Diletta Mio is everything a classic Italian-made espresso machine should be. It's compact, stylish, built to last, and brews circles around the competition. It's also a simple joy to use, wrote former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey. It feels a bit analog, like an heirloom-quality stand mixer, but also sports sophisticated features like a PID (proportional-integral-derivative) temperature controller—a wee processor with an algorithm that keeps brew temperatures stable. Among traditional espresso machines that require a separate grinder, this is the one WIRED recommends.

Sources indicate that upgrade: WIRED's upgrade pick, the Diletta Bello ($1,899), is for advanced beanheads who love a sensitive machine. On the Bello, every difference makes a difference: every micron of grind size, or slight gradation of tamping pressure, will produce a different cup of espresso. But when you've dialed in your bean, the Bello is beautifully faithful—offering shot after shot of caramely crema and rich espresso.

Industry observers note that the Bambino is little, fast, low-cost, and convenient—about as wide as a one-dollar bill. There are no apparent frills and no grinder: just a steam wand for silky milk and a choice between single or double shots. But look under the hood of this $300 beauty and you'll note features that are hallmarks of much more expensive machines: a thermoblock for immediate heating and a PID (proportional, integral, derivative) temperature controller that makes for consistent brew temps usually out of reach at this price range.

It has been revealed that which is to say it's a wee machine that pulls far above its weight class. Pair your Bambino with a good mid-level grinder and you'll be making beautiful cups with counter space to spare, for a total of $500.

Upgrade: The Breville Bambino Plus ($500) is hardier and slightly bigger and offers automatic milk frothing.

The Rancilio Silvia Pro is one of WIRED's longtime favorite dual-boiler espresso machines, packed with pro-level features and built to last seemingly forever, with few plastic parts. For far less than half the price, there's the Silvia M: the sleek, smaller-footprint, single-boiler cousin. What's the diff? There'll be a little bit more lag time between shots, if multiple people want espresso immediately. But you'll get that same high-quality metal build, and consistent water temp and steam pressure. This means well-extracted, café-grade espresso.

Industry observers note that note that the Silvia is notoriously sensitive, so it's not for beginners. It's also famously long-lasting, repairable, and able to be endlessly modified, and so it's birthed its own society of cult devotees. Just like buying a Land Cruiser or a Jeep, you'll end up with new friends. And if people online are to be believed, a lot of the OG Silvias have been chugging along for literal decades.

In a recent development, it's tough to find a reliable espresso machine in the $200 range—and Italian coffee machine company De'Longhi has long dominated the WIRED Gear team's favorite no-nonsense, low-budget espresso picks. The newly introduced De'Longhi Classic (previously branded as “Linea Classic”) is shiny chrome, with buttons for steam and your choice of single or double shots. It likewise sports a rare-at-this-price-point pressure gauge, a 15-bar pump, and an updated thermoblock system for fast heating.

The small touches matter. The steam wand has enough oomph to create some rudimentary latte art, if that’s your thing. And there's enough clearance between the portafilter and drip tray to fit a coffee or cappuccino mug, as opposed to a tiny espresso cup. But this noted, after learning a few fun tricks from coffee influencer Lance Hedrick, I'm now also revisiting our previous extreme budget pick, De'Longhi Stilosa.

Sources indicate that this guide is mostly dedicated to machines that make more classic espresso—the finicky kind that's harder to navigate and might leave coffee grounds on your counter. This sophisticated bean-to-cup De'Longhi Rivelia is a little different. It's my top pick among super-automatic machines that'll have you just fill a hopper with a half-bag of beans, then press a button. After helping you choose the right grinder settings, and asking how you like your coffee among well more than a dozen options, this touchscreen device will grind, and brew, and then froth up your milk for you.

In a recent development, even the milk frother is about the easiest I've used, and it works with a single button-press once you've adjusted the foam density for drinks from dense flat white to frothy cappuccino. Heck, my mom was able to figure it out within a day, and so was my father. Even better, the Rivelia offers two swappable bean hoppers, an unheard-of luxury among similar devices that'll allow you to switch easily to decaf late in the day.

Note, however, that automatic machines like this Rivelia tend to make somewhat different coffee from what you'll get from other machines on this list. It grinds a bit coarser, leading to less unpredictability but also less intensity. If you're a milk lover, this likely won't matter much—and you may instead prize the simple ease with which you can have a frothing latte. Vodka lovers will find the same, when mixing cold espresso shots with the device.

Sources indicate that ever wonder why an espresso shot is sometimes called a pull? In the beginning, baristas used a lever to create the necessary pressure to extract espresso. And there's still a real satisfaction to literally pulling your own espresso, reviewer Jaina Grey noted. There’s no milk steamer, no boiler, no power cable. This thing is powered by a human, namely you.

Load it up with coffee and water per the manufacturer’s instructions and give it a good press. There’s also a pressure gauge to make sure you're hitting the target. Think of it like one of those strongman games at a carnival, except that the reward is delicious espresso.

How Do I Test Espresso Machines?

Industry observers note that over the past decade, WIRED has tested dozens of espresso makers to find our favorites. The process, in part, is simple. We brew a whole lot of coffee. I’ve written about coffee for more than a decade on both the East and West Coasts, including my hometown coffee mecca of Portland, Oregon. Other current and past WIRED espresso testers—who include former baristas and longtime coffee writers—include Jaina Grey, Jeffrey Van Camp, Kat Merck, Tyler Shane, Pete Cottell, and Scott Gilbertson.

In a recent development, on each machine that’s capable, I make and assess at least four styles of drink, on multiple roasts and beans: a basic 2:1 espresso, an Americano, a latte, and a cappuccino. On machines that advertise a wacky array of drinks, I test each one. This includes any newfangled coldspresso and head-scratching variations on a “long.” It also includes, if science dictates, espresso martinis. And I test to see whether a machine can be dialed to both dark roasts and lighter roasts.

I might make many dozens of coffees to dial in a machine and truly understand it, and on any of my top picks I've made at least fifty drinks. Sometimes, alas, you understand a machine’s shortcomings far sooner—and so some of our less-recommended devices are dismissed a bit earlier.

What I’m looking for is nuance, aromatics, beauty, sensitivity to the characteristics of each bean, and the satisfying texture of fully integrated milk. But also, I’m looking for ease, the thoughtful touches that make an espresso maker something you can fall in love with.

Industry observers note that I test whether the hot water spout splatters, whether descaling requires a degree in hydrology, whether the brewing temperature is consistent, and whether the latte milk gets silked. I’m truly terrible at latte art, but whether it’s possible is a straightforward test of the body of the frothed milk. I test the airier foam of cappuccinos and compare manual and automatic milk frothing on machines that try to froth milk for you. I test how fast the wand steams and whether it’s easy to fully integrate milk before the dang thing starts to burn your milk.

Industry observers note that on machines with built-in grinders, I both assess the grind and weigh the dose—and then weigh it again. And then again. Consistency is the hobgoblin of little cups. I also test multiple grind settings to make sure the grind is consistent.

It has been revealed that on any semiautomatic machine that decides the shot size for you, I test this to see whether you're getting a ristretto or a lungo by default. Then I resolve never to say the word “lungo” again.

I don’t generally take apart the machines I’m sent, but I do quite often look up videos of people who do—and look at how the thing’s constructed under the hood.

How I Select Espresso Machines to Review.

In a recent development, in part, we select machines to test by looking at the espresso makers with long track records of making good espresso machines—people with long tails in the industry and good track records of customer support. Names like Breville, De'Longhi, La Marzocco, and Rancilio. But also, I listen. I read. I ask every coffee-obsessive in my life. I pay attention to the newest releases, follow trade shows, watch Youtube videos, and spend a lot of time tracking down not just the obious big names but the unexpected recommendations.

Sources indicate that I often also look at how accessible each machine will be to most people. Espresso isn’t just a finicky process: It’s finicky by design. The most sensitive and sophisticated traditional machines are responsive to every tiny variation in the coffee grind and every fluctuation in the water temperature. The deepest bean geeks want this: They want the control, the frustration, the vision quest.

But I also know that most of you out there aren’t looking to be in an abusive relationship with your coffee machine. Few want to wake up to feelings of inadequacy, brought on by a machine that costs as much as a used car. And so what I look for is the espresso machines that can pull lovely character from each bean, but also make this easy on you.

This means that our top picks, the ones I recommend to most people, tend to fall in the semiautomatic camp: They’re the ones that offer the best coffee with the least effort. Finding this balance is delicate and often rewarding. It used to be that a built-in grinder was a recipe for blown shots, sadness, or pressurized portafilters with less character. But year by year, espresso machine makers get better at this goal.

The lowest-cost machines I recommend tend to offer more forgiving pressurized filter baskets as options, even though these sacrifice a bit of nuance for forgiveness, because I don’t want to assume you’re pairing a $200 espresso machine with a $2,000 coffee grinder. Although I know some of you do this, especially with our beloved Breville Bambino.

Industry observers note that but hey, if you’re a tinkerer for life, and want to join modding groups? We recommend a machine for you, too. Mostly so you can disagree on Reddit, and explain why your favorite is better.

What Beans Are Best for Espresso?

First off, there's no such thing as “espresso beans,” whatever it says on the bag you buy. Espresso beans are coffee beans, ground finely enough to be pressed into service as espresso.

But traditionally, espresso is made with darker-roast beans that best elicit the deep, chocolatey notes of classic Italian espresso. In fact, most machines you use are probably designed with dark-roast beans in mind: Darker beans grind easier, extract easier, and are a bit more homogeneous across the market. And so when someone writes “espresso roast” or “espresso blend” on their grind, that's often what they mean.

It has been revealed that does that mean dark roast is the only espresso? Of course not. Modern craft and premium coffee roasters in the United States have begun trending toward medium and medium-dark roasts that offer a bit more balance, character, and even a little acidity—beans that have more aromatics, and more individuality. Some, including me, love experimenting with truly light roasts, including the lightest of natural-processed beans that let me brew up espresso that tastes like strawberries.

In a recent development, it's up to you. But note that the lighter the roast, the more you'll need to adjust grind and temperature to accommodate—and sometimes even go off-script entirely. (See here for an explainer on light-roast espresso.) But the classic recommendations for espresso? Pulling a 25- to 30-second shot, at a steady 9 bars of pressure, at a 2:1 ratio for a standard shot? These were all designed for traditional dark-roast beans.

It has been revealed that one thing that's true, however, is that you should use fresh beans. They'll taste better and more aromatic, sure. But stale beans exposed to oxygen also make it technically difficult to make good espresso: they've begun to break down, often allow channeling, and are more likely to lead to a less evenly extracted shot with funny off-flavors.

Obviously, fresh beans are easiest to obtain from a local roaster, and on the plus side you'll be able to ask the baristas there how best to make espresso from their beans. But when in doubt in a supermarket, look for a roast date on the bag. If you can't find it, or if your beans were roasted in Italy and sent on a ship? Chances are they're not fresh. And your espresso will be worse. For fresh beans delivered to your house, check out WIRED's guide to the best coffee subscriptions.

Espresso Accessories That Make for Great Cups.

If you're spending this much on an espresso machine, you'll want to invest in a good grinder and even a scale, as well as a few other devices that make your shots better, and your life a little easier.

Recent findings suggest that an espresso-capable grinder: If your espresso machine doesn't come with a grinder, you'll need one. Preground bag beans are especially difficult to use when making espresso, and will likely lead to off-flavors or channeling. But not just any grinder will do. You'll need a good grinder that can grind consistent beans finely enough for espresso. WIRED's top-pick Baratza Encore ESP is always a good choice—positioned squarely at the fulcrum where more expensive grinders begin to offer diminishing returns.

An accurate scale with a timer: Most grinders, and a goodly portion of espresso machines, do not offer a precise scale. But a precise scale is what you need to get espresso ratios right. WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu loved the Acaia brew-by-weight scale ($400) that automatically connects to the La Marzocco Linea Mini and a few other devices via its companion app. But a far less sophisticated scale can still help you measure your shot size and control the dose you want on each espresso shot. If you're not precious about beauty, there's always this low-cost, little no-name scale. It's accurate to a 10th of a gram, and has a timer to boot.

It has been revealed that the best knockbox: When you're done with that portafilter filled with coffee grounds, what do you do with it? Beat it against the side of a trashcan? Dig out those grounds into the sink? Nah. You need a good knock box. And somehow this jobby-job from Breville is the best one I've ever found. It's sturdy, the cross bar is in the right spot so that the grinds dump cleanly into the bin, and the bottom has enough grip that the box doesn't scoot around on the counter. Simplicity is competence.

In a recent development, not all steaming pitchers are created equal, notes WIRED contributing reviewer (and former barista) Pete Cottell. As opposed to the sad piece of aluminum that probably came with your espresso maker, this Brewista offers thick walls for heat retention, a precision tip for expert latte pours, and a thermometer sticker on its side so you can get a rough gauge of milk temperature without hunting down an actual thermometer. It can also take a beating. This is your fresh frothing pitcher.

It has been revealed that breville Oracle Jet for $2,000: The Breville Oracle Jet is my previous top pick for threading that delicate needle between ease and deliciousness, before getting displaced by my new top-pick Fellow device. The Oracle Jet remains a powerful and frankly beautiful stainless-steel machine, with sterling temperature control and a solid built-in grinder that uses the same conical burrs as the excellent Baratza Encore ESP ($200). This Oracle Jet will pull beautiful nuances from beans ranging from berry-light to chocolate dark, on drinks ranging from an Americano to a flat white to “cold espresso” best placed in a martini. And yet the Jet's easily accessible for anyone who can figure out an iPhone, with a touchscreen tutorial, digital guidance on finding the right grind for each bean, and automatic tamping and steaming. You'll be nose-deep in a cappuccino within 20 minutes of pulling this thing out of the box. Note that manual milk steaming with the Jet's powerful wand is still better than the automatic version.

It has been revealed that ninja Luxe Cafe Pro for $750: Tradition is the opposite of what Ninja does. This is the company that made the soft-serve Swirl, the Slushi, and the portable air fryer. Ninja is all about the extras. And Ninja doesn't judge. And so of course Ninja jumped in with both feet on cold-foam coldspresso. In fact, the fresh Luxe Cafe Pro makes the best cold foam out of any espresso machine I've tried, with a whisk that whips up plant milk or cow milk into thick, creamy, dense, beautiful froth—ready for your ridiculously complicated cold caramel-vanilla latte TikTok recipe. What I didn't expect was that Ninja would also nail the fundamentals so well, on only its second entry into the espresso market. The relatively accurate by-weight dosing is nice. So is the excellent steam wand that also outpaces most contenders on automatic hot foaming, adjustable to multiple densities of foam. The Pro clears up some oversights in the previous-model Premier, including an easy tamping lever, and a hot water spout. Maintenance, whether descaling or purging, is also as easy as it gets. Just don't use this grinder with light roast beans. Medium or dark only.

It has been revealed that breville Oracle Dual Boiler for $3,000: This enhancement to the previous Breville Dual Boiler espresso machine is a powerful, truly impressive machine in many regards. It combines the easy touchscreen operation and automatic dosing and tamping of WIRED's previous top-pick Oracle Jet with a welcome “manual” mode that lets you play with pre-infusion and bloom while monitoring a digital pressure gauge on the touchscreen. I kinda love this as an exercise in future-retro design—or whatever the inverse of steampunk is—but also as a means of really controlling my shot, and getting a lot more crema and body out of it. The dual boiler heats up very fast—like four minutes fast—and gives you the wonderful temperature stability and consistency you expect from a dual boiler, plus the ability to steam milk and make espresso simultaneously. The production model I received had a very tight portafilter fit, which loosened up after the first 30 shots or so but initially required some muscle. I also haven't been able to get good results with lighter-roast beans, which led to the occasional under-filled portafilter that had to be retamped manually. We'll update as we resolve those quirks, but can attest that for medium to dark beans, this Dual Boiler is an absolute beast.

Meraki Espresso Machine for $1,999: When former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage first tested this high-design “steampunk gasworks” of an espresso machine, he loved the features for the price, including a Timemore grinder that grinds by weight, PID temperature control, easy pre-infusion, and another scale under the brewer that lets you control output. He did not, however, love having to overrotate the portafilter for a proper fit, or the wackily complicated descaling procedure. I’ve since tested the second run of this machine (the one you’ll be getting if you buy right now) and did not have any trouble with the portafilter. You’ll also get 45 grind settings instead of the original 30, though we were hard-pressed to discern a real difference from the additional 15. —Kat Merck.

According to recent reports, ninja Luxe Cafe Premier for $600: Ninja has already released an upgraded Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro version ($750) after its espresso machine debut. But its first device, the Luxe Cafe Premier, is already a corker, a low-priced all-in-one with cold brew, coffee, espresso, excellent milk frothing, and unexpected luxury features like a built-in scale so the grinder can dose by weight. The device can feel either overstuffed or generous, depending on who you are. Either way, this damn near unseated the Breville Barista Express as WIRED’s mid-tier top pick, aside from a few leaks and sensible caution about its durability.

De'Longhi La Specialista Opera for $800: Speaking of espresso makers that came running at Breville, this Opera is a beautifully forgiving semiautomatic machine that makes excellent espresso in the medium- to dark-roast range, with non-pressurized portafilter baskets that make for a nice and surprisingly subtle cup. It’s the best De'Longhi espresso machine I’ve tested, in many ways, among the semiautomatic camp. The Opera sports a lot of options—including dose and temperature control—while remaining refreshingly analog with its satisfying metal frame, metal buttons, and prominent pressure gauge. Cold brew is a perk for those who like milk. The grinder is decent, though its 15 settings might not offer enough sensitivity to pull the best from each roast. One could wish for a removable hopper and a sturdier tamping lever. But if you or your partner love cold coffee drinks or espresso martinis, this gives comparable Brevilles a strong run for the money.

De'Longhi La Specialista Touch for $800: De'Longhi’s newly introduced Touch, released this year, isn't merely a touchscreen version of the very analog Opera—though it is just as handsome as the Opera. Instead, it offers a very specific set of trade-offs. Like De'Longhi's Rivelia, there's a bean-assist function that you can save for each bean you like. It also has a better steam wand, with the ability to read the temperature of the milk you're steaming as you steam it. In fact, it's maybe more intuitive overall. But it doesn't quite offer the easy customization on temperature, shot time, or ratios. The cold brew is not quite as well-dialed as the Opera. The Touch is an Italian machine on training wheels, designed for Italian-style medium to dark shots. This should work for most people, but minus a pressure bar or a shot timer, it can also feel like a bit of a black box.

Recent findings suggest that la Marzocco Linea Mini for $6,600: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu spent two weeks with La Marzocco's Linea Mini, a home version of the fancy espresso machines you'll see in coffee shops around the world. The price may be eye-searing, but Chokkattu did find the resulting elixir to be absolutely fantastic—and the same went for La Marzocco's customer service while Chokkattu was dialing in his machine. It offers a lot of room for experimentation, and it sports a killer cool-touch steam wand that froths milk in seconds.

De'Longhi Stilosa for $150: The Stilosa was our top budget pick for years. It's still a good budget pick, and it often goes on sale for less than $100. You're not going to get high-end features like a pressure gauge or built-in grinder, and it's a little plasticky. But what the Stilosa does provide is everything you need to make great espresso at home: a solid portafilter, a reliable steam pump, and a steaming wand. It is a little light, so you'll want to brace it when you mount and dismount the portafilter (or it might slide around on you). After brewing cup after cup of espresso, the Stilosa never highlighted signs of slowing or breaking down the way many inexpensive machines can. In fact, we're now revisiting the Stilosa as our budget pick, after catching a few tips on how to use the Stilosa for light roast espresso.

According to recent reports, breville Barista Express Impress for $800: This espresso machine is the more tricked-out sibling of the Breville Barista Express. It includes more grind and dosing settings and automates some of the more complicated parts of brewing consistently good espresso, like getting just the right amount of beans ground per shot.

In a recent development, breville Dual Boiler for $1,600: The previous-generation Breville Dual Boiler is an absolute tank of an espresso machine. It's huge. It's heavy. It makes amazing espresso. But while its size makes brewing espresso feel luxurious, it does eat up a lot of space and needs a little time to heat up, versus newer Brevilles like the Oracle Jet that favor thermoblock-style heaters. But a dual boiler does mean you can brew shot after shot, with steamed milk and hot water at the same time, without having to wait in between shots. The fresh Breville Oracle Dual Boiler ($3,000) is already on the market, but you can still pick up the previous generation for half the price.

In a recent development, cuisinart EM-160 Slim for $250: The lowest-cost espresso maker from Cuisinart's new espresso line is among the slimmer espresso machines out there, less than 7 inches across. This makes it a treasure for certain kitchens. The espresso quality is about what you'd expect from a pressurized portafilter: smoother, less nuanced, but also pretty forgiving for beginners trying to dial in a bean. This'll be best for those who mix milk with their espresso. Same goes for the fast-dripped “cold espresso” option, which takes a couple minutes to complete and comes out a bit tannic, but mixes well with cold milk or a lot of ice. You'll need a grinder if you don't want sad supermarket beans.

Superkop Manual Espresso Maker for $800: This manual espresso machine is technically not a Jackie Chan movie. The Superkop is instead a quite finely engineered espresso device. It looks pretty, and unlike other manual espresso machines, you don't need a strong arm to use it. So if you want to pull espresso, but not pull it hard, the Superkop is your huckleberry. That said, $600 is a lot of money for a manual device. Buy it if you know you'll love it.

Gevi Espresso Machine With Grinder and Milk Frother for $350: WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell prized the pressure control and built-in grinder on this Gevi espresso machine, when you take into account the near-unfathomable low price for a machine with this functionality. Alas, a somewhat erratic steam wand makes it hard to recommend.

Cuisinart EM-640 Espresso Bar for $650: Cuisinart rolled in with some ambition on this semiautomatic espresso machine, with a built-in grinder and a non-pressurized, bottomless portafilter meant to play in the same sandbox as Breville's top devices. Alas, I really couldn't get consistency on either dosing or grinding from the device's built-in grinder—and the system for customizing the dose in particular was mostly wild guesswork. This all added up to botched shots, wild spray from the portafilter, and none of the ease one wants from a semiautomatic.

De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $700: This semiautomatic De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo comes with a built-in burr grinder and makes great espresso right out of the box, and is slimmer than other espresso machines in its category. It does have quirks: It includes a little plastic adapter needed to attach the portafilter to the grinder spout, and a little stepstool for your espresso cup to keep the coffee from splashing. It’s a good machine, but I'd upgrade to the Opera any day of the week.

Breaking: Trump halts Iowa detonation, notes new governor to blame if it blows accidentally

💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa.
  • According to recent reports, the Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups.
  • Sources indicate that iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, who won’t be sworn into office until January.

According to recent reports, the Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).

Sources indicate that iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.

Industry observers note that late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice’s request to put a hold on the Army’s permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle stated the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and prepares.

According to recent reports, documents released by the Army last week said that the military first learned in March that the lead azide had started to degrade and crystallize. Lead azide is used in detonators for munitions, but in crystallized form it becomes highly unstable and sensitive to physical movement or friction. The IAAAP is said to contain around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of lead azide in barrels held in earth-covered containers.

In a recent development, in late March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions to safely dispose of the lead azide, according to a Upcoming York Times report. MuniRem uses a sulfur-based solution that reportedly breaks down explosives and immobilizes toxic chemicals, eliminating the need for detonation. The company had proposed spraying the inside of the earth-covered containers housing the barrels as well as the barrel surfaces to neutralize risks of spontaneous explosions.

In a recent development, but two months later, the Army canceled the contract without explanation. An Army contracting officer told MuniRem in an email at the time that the cancellation “was not based on deficiencies” in MuniRem’s looks, the Times reported. The company’s founder noted MuniRem filed public records requests to get more information on why the contract was scrapped, but it has not received a response.

Now, the Army claims that the lead azide has only degraded further since March and that it cannot move the barrels or even open their lids without risking a catastrophic explosion. Further, it claims that winter temperatures in the coming days increase the risk of spontaneous detonation.

“As the temperatures drop, the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures,” lawyers for the Trump administration wrote in a court filing over the weekend. “If the crystals break, this could cause a chain reaction detonation that could cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the environment.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Army claims that the only choice now is between a controlled, mitigated explosion or an uncontrolled, unmitigated explosion. In court filings this weekend, government lawyers argued that the Army does not need the now-suspended EPA permit to move forward with the detonation, because the Army has determined that the lead azide poses an “immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”.

Last Thursday, Telle mentioned that the delay until Monday was the “latest possible moment” for a controlled detonation before temperatures dropped dangerously low. But the military subsequently delayed the detonation again until Tuesday and then pushed it back to Wednesday.

Industry observers note that in his social media post Monday, Trump stated he thought carrying out the controlled detonation was the “proper course.” But he said he was making the decision the responsibility of the federal appeals court and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat. If the lead azide spontaneously detonates on their watch, Trump claimed, they will be fully to blame.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump wrote.

In a social media post Sunday evening, Sand called for answers on how the situation was able to become so dangerous, specifically raising the question of why MuniRem’s contract was canceled.

“Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again,” he wrote.
